verdicts.why: Factually wrong that the declaration drives allocation: line 145 creates an EMPTY HashMap, and entries only materialize from bytes actually read through the TruncatedInputStream budget built at lines 146-147, so growth is NOT 'regardless of frame size' — each entry costs >=2 wire bytes and readShortstr/readFieldValue throw EOFException when the bytes run out.

The overflow grants the attacker nothing: the seconds value at line 269 is fully attacker-chosen, so 'stale/future-dated messages' are reachable with any in-range value without overflow, and every input that does overflow (>9.2e15 seconds, ~292 million years) already yields a nonsensical Date whether it wraps or not.

The stated impact is impossible: readFieldValue begins with in.readUnsignedByte() (line 161), which consumes exactly one byte or throws EOFException, so every iteration of the line-244 loop strictly shrinks the TruncatedInputStream budget and the loop must terminate — there is no infinite loop.

Not a defect: line 151's containsKey guard is a deterministic first-wins disambiguation of a duplicate key, and the entire asserted impact is the absence of a log/exception/counter, with no attacker capability and no state corruption identified.

Factually wrong: InputStream.read() returns 0..255 for a data byte (0xFF yields 255) and -1 only at EOF, so the two are perfectly distinguishable, and the OR-then-sign-test at line 231 catches any -1 because the sign bit propagates; the claim itself concedes 'the logic is correct'.

Could not refute: line 88 allocates new byte[(int)contentLength] BEFORE readFully at line 89 can fail, so a 4-byte wire length of up to Integer.MAX_VALUE-1 forces a ~2GB heap allocation attempt from 4 attacker-controlled bytes; the only guard (line 87) rejects >=Integer.MAX_VALUE and nothing else caps it.

Both bounds it says are missing are enforced: line 172's readUnsignedByte() confines scale to 0..255 so it can never exceed Integer.MAX_VALUE or go negative, and line 173 fixes the unscaled magnitude at exactly 4 bytes, so the BigInteger/BigDecimal at line 175 is not 'unbounded'.

The line-68 anchor is a non-issue (readUnsignedByte bounds it to 255, as the claim itself concedes), but the operative assertion holds: line 88 allocates new byte[(int)contentLength] from a wire-supplied length with only the line-87 <Integer.MAX_VALUE check, permitting a ~2GB allocation before any data is read.

No mechanism for the asserted HIGH impact: the wrapped product at line 269 is not used in any comparison, authorization or scheduling decision in this file, and 'timing-based attacks' is unsupported — the attacker already picks the timestamp outright, so wrapping adds no capability.

The central assertion is false: if any of the four read() calls returns -1, the OR at line 231 has its sign bit set and EOFException is always thrown — there is no branch where a partial read yields a non-negative value; readInt() is equally non-atomic, so the 'race condition' point does not distinguish it.

Factual error about the code and self-contradictory: line 151 is 'if(!table.containsKey(name))', so duplicates never overwrite the earlier value — the FIRST value is kept, the exact opposite of the claim's title and impact.

Line 172's in.readUnsignedByte() can never return a negative value, so the 'extremely large negative scale' premise is unreachable; additionally BigDecimal(BigInteger,int) stores scale as a field and allocates nothing proportional to it, so the memory-exhaustion mechanism does not exist.

UTF-8 is mandated on every JVM so 'utf-8' at line 70 cannot be unavailable, and UnsupportedEncodingException is an IOException subclass already covered by the method's 'throws IOException' at line 66 — propagation is handling; no impact is stated for lenient decoding of malformed sequences.

A readability preference that concedes 'the logic is correct', with no attacker and no impact; it is also factually wrong that readInt() is equivalent — readInt() returns a signed int, whereas lines 227-233 must produce an unsigned 32-bit value widened into a long.

Could not refute: case 'F' (line 181) calls readTable which re-enters readFieldValue (line 150), and case 'A' (line 184) calls readArray which re-enters it (line 245), with no depth parameter or counter anywhere in the file; each nesting level costs only ~5 wire bytes, so a modest frame reaches thousands of frames of recursion.

Not a defect with any consequence: overflow at line 269 requires a seconds value above ~9.2e15 (~292 million years), which already produces a meaningless Date without wrapping, and the value is attacker-chosen either way, so nothing downstream behaves differently.

The bound is enforced by the read itself: in.readUnsignedByte() at line 172 yields 0..255, so the cited 'scale of Integer.MAX_VALUE' is unreachable, and BigDecimal stores that scale as a plain field with no computation, so there is no performance or precision effect.

Whether available() can report 0 while bytes remain depends on TruncatedInputStream.available() and on what underlying stream the caller passes to the public ValueReader(DataInputStream) constructor (line 57); neither TruncatedInputStream.java nor any caller is present in the target, so the premature-exit premise cannot be settled from these files.

Factually wrong that exhaustion hangs: DataInputStream.readFully throws EOFException when the stream ends before the buffer is filled, so lines 69/89/174 only block if the socket blocks — and a socket timeout can only be set on the stream the caller hands to the constructor at line 57, not by a value parser that never sees a socket.

The bound is enforced at lines 146-147: entries are added only for pairs actually parsed out of the TruncatedInputStream budget, each costing >=2 wire bytes, so the map cannot 'grow unbounded' — the claim's own example (1MB of fields) yields on the order of tens of MB, growth proportional to input rather than heap exhaustion from a declaration.

Same crux as C18: the accuracy of available() at lines 148 and 244 is a property of TruncatedInputStream and of whatever stream the caller supplies, and neither file is included in the target, so it cannot be decided here.

A pure style/micro-optimization note with no attacker and no impact; it is also factually off — the JDK caches charset lookups, so line 70 does not re-parse the name on every call, and a misspelling would fail on the first invocation, not silently.

Could not refute: line 181 (case 'F' -> readTable -> readFieldValue at line 150) and line 184 (case 'A' -> readArray -> readFieldValue at line 245) form an unguarded recursion cycle, and the file contains no depth parameter, counter or limit of any kind.

Not a defect: the streams at lines 146-147 and 241-242 are filters over the caller's already-open 'in' and open no resource of their own, so closing them would close the caller's connection stream — a bug, not a fix; the 'if TruncatedInputStream opens underlying resources' premise is speculation contradicted by the constructor argument.

Could not refute: readFieldValue re-enters itself through readTable (line 181 -> line 150) and readArray (line 184 -> line 245) with no recursion guard, and nothing in the file caps nesting depth, so deeply nested tables/arrays reach StackOverflowError.

Nothing is pre-allocated from the declared length: the ArrayList at line 243 starts empty and grows only per element actually parsed from the TruncatedInputStream budget (lines 241-242), and the cheapest element ('V', 1 wire byte) costs only a few bytes of heap, so there is no amplification that turns a declared length into exhaustion.

Backwards: 'contentLength < Integer.MAX_VALUE' at line 87 EXCLUDES Integer.MAX_VALUE, so that exact value takes the else branch and throws UnsupportedOperationException at line 92 — it never reaches the cast; the claim's own evidence then admits the int cast does not overflow.

The asserted impact cannot occur: readFieldValue's first act is in.readUnsignedByte() (line 161), which consumes a byte or throws EOFException, so the line-148 loop strictly drains a finite budget and can neither loop forever nor 'behave unpredictably'; a short read would surface as EOFException, not silent misparse.
